Findings
========

1. Blocking / performance  
   • The requests are executed **sequentially** (`for-await` loop + `await fetch`).  
   • If you have 50 URLs the total latency = Σ each request time instead of max(request time).

2. Missing error handling  
   • `fetch()` can throw (network failure, invalid URL).  
   • `res.ok` is never checked; you will happily call `res.json()` on a 404/500 body.  
   • `res.json()` will itself throw if the body is not valid JSON.  
   • One failure aborts the whole function and loses everything fetched so far.

3. No timeout / abort logic  
   • `fetch` has no default timeout; a hanging server can keep the promise open forever.

4. Potential security issues (when this code runs on the server)  
   • SSRF – nothing prevents a caller from passing `http://127.0.0.1:27017/…` etc.  
   • Open redirect / malicious URL strings could crash the function (`new URL(...)` throws).  
   • Unvalidated JSON is blindly trusted; if you later stringify it you can hit JSON-injection
     (e.g. `<script>/* … */`).  
   • If you rely on cookies/credentials you should pass `credentials:'same-origin'` or
     `'include'`; otherwise you may leak or miss auth information.

5. Memory pressure  
   • All responses are buffered into memory before you return.  Large payloads ⇒ OOM.  
   • If you only need a subset or can stream, consider `response.body`.

6. Readability / API design  
   • Missing JSDoc / TypeScript typing – consumers don’t know what shape `urls` or
     `results` are.  
   • No way to configure headers, request method, concurrency, etc.

How to fix / improve
====================

A. Parallelise but keep order
-----------------------------
Use `Promise.all`, or a concurrency-limiter such as `p-limit` so you don’t DDOS the
remote server.

```
import pLimit from 'p-limit';

async function fetchAll(urls, {
  concurrency = 8,
  timeout    = 10_000,       // ms
  allowedHosts = []          // restrict targets if running on the server
} = {}) {

  const limit = pLimit(concurrency);

  const tasks = urls.map(urlStr =>
    limit(() => safeFetchJson(urlStr, timeout, allowedHosts))
  );

  return Promise.all(tasks);   // preserves order
}
```

B. Safer single-request helper
------------------------------

```
async function safeFetchJson(urlStr, timeout, allowedHosts) {
  // ---- basic SSRF mitigation ------------------------------------------------
  const url = new URL(urlStr);
  if (allowedHosts.length && !allowedHosts.includes(url.hostname)) {
    throw new Error(`Host ${url.hostname} is not allowed`);
  }

  // ---- timeout / abort ------------------------------------------------------
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeout);

  try {
    const res = await fetch(url.href, {
      signal: controller.signal,
      headers: { 'Accept': 'application/json' },
      credentials: 'same-origin'
    });

    if (!res.ok) {                        // HTTP 2xx guard
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status} for ${url.href}`);
    }

    return await res.json();              // may still throw → caught below
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}
```

C. Consumer-side error visibility
---------------------------------
If you want the whole batch to succeed or fail atomically, let the error bubble
out (`Promise.all` will reject).  
If you prefer “best effort”, catch inside the task and return e.g.

```
return { url: urlStr, ok: false, error: err.message };
```

D. Optional streaming for large bodies
--------------------------------------
Instead of `res.json()` you can stream/iterate `res.body`, or use
`Response.json()` with a reviver that discards what you don’t need.

E. Documentation / Types
------------------------
Add:

```ts
/**
 * Fetch a list of URLs and parse each response as JSON.
 * @param {string[]} urls
 * @param {{ concurrency?: number, timeout?: number, allowedHosts?: string[] }} [options]
 * @returns {Promise<any[]>}
 */
```

F. Testing
----------
Have unit tests that stub `fetch` and assert:

* All URLs are requested.
* Non-2xx status raises.
* Invalid JSON raises.
* Concurrency limit is respected.

Summary
-------
Original code is simple but:

• Slow (serial).  
• Brittle (no error or status check).  
• Unsafe for server use (SSRF, no timeout).  

Adopt parallel fetching with limits, robust error/timeout handling, optional host
whitelisting, and document the API to make it production-ready.
